lessons.title: Types of Growth Promotants: Implants and Beta-Agonists
lessons.body: Growth promotants are tools that help cattle grow faster and convert feed more efficiently. In steer fattening, the two main types used in Africa are hormonal implants and beta-agonists. Hormonal implants are small pellets placed under the skin of the ear. They release natural or synthetic hormones like estradiol, testosterone, or progesterone. These hormones tell the steer's body to deposit more lean muscle and less fat. Common brands include Revalor, Synovex, and Compudose. For example, a single Revalor-S implant can increase daily weight gain by 0.2 to 0.3 kg and improve feed efficiency by 8-12% over 90 to 120 days. Implants are widely used in South Africa, Namibia, and Botswana, but are banned in the European Union. Beta-agonists are feed additives, not implants. They are drugs like zilpaterol (Zilmax) and ractopamine (Paylean). They are fed during the last 20 to 40 days before slaughter. They redirect nutrients to muscle growth, increasing carcass weight by 5 to 15 kg and improving feed efficiency. However, beta-agonists are controversial. Ractopamine is banned in the EU, China, and Russia. In Africa, only South Africa has approved zilpaterol for use under strict withdrawal periods. Many small-scale farmers avoid both implants and beta-agonists because of market restrictions and consumer concerns. Instead, they focus on good nutrition, health, and genetics. If you plan to use growth promotants, first check your local regulations and your buyer's requirements. For example, if you sell to a local butcher who exports to Europe, you cannot use implants or beta-agonists. If you sell to a local feedlot or butcher within South Africa, you may use them legally. Always keep records of what you use and when. This helps you avoid residue problems and meet market demands. Remember, growth promotants are not a substitute for poor management. They work best when cattle are healthy, well-fed, and have good genetics.

lessons.title: Regulations and Residue Avoidance
lessons.body: Using growth promotants without following regulations can get you into serious trouble. In Africa, rules differ by country. South Africa allows hormonal implants and beta-agonists like zilpaterol, but only with a veterinary prescription and strict withdrawal periods. Namibia and Botswana allow implants but not beta-agonists. Kenya, Nigeria, and most other African countries ban hormonal implants entirely. The European Union bans all hormonal implants and beta-agonists, and any meat exported there must be free of residues. Residues are traces of the drug left in the meat. To avoid residues, you must follow the withdrawal period exactly. For implants, there is no withdrawal period because the hormones are released slowly and are natural. For beta-agonists like zilpaterol, the withdrawal period is typically 3 to 7 days before slaughter. If you slaughter too early, the drug will still be in the meat. This can cause health problems for consumers and lead to rejected carcasses. Always read the label and follow your veterinarian's advice. Keep a record for each animal: date implanted or fed, product name, dose, and withdrawal end date. Use a calendar or notebook. Before selling, check that the withdrawal period has passed. If you sell to a feedlot or abattoir, they will test for residues. If found, you may be fined or banned from selling. In some countries, residue testing is done at slaughterhouses. For example, South Africa's meat safety scheme tests for zilpaterol residues. If you are unsure about regulations, ask your local extension officer or veterinarian. Never use products meant for other animals. Never increase the dose. Never implant into the muscle or fat instead of the ear. The ear is the only approved site because it is discarded at slaughter. If you implant elsewhere, residues can remain in the meat. Also, do not use implants on dairy cows or breeding animals. They are only for steers and heifers destined for meat. Following the rules protects your reputation, your buyers, and your community.

lessons.title: Implanting Techniques and Timing
lessons.body: Implanting is a simple procedure, but it must be done correctly to work and to avoid problems. You need a clean implant gun, a sharp needle, and the implants themselves. Common implant guns include the Synovex gun or the Revalor gun. Before you start, restrain the steer in a head gate or crush. Clean the ear with a disinfectant like iodine. The implant site is the middle third of the ear, between the skin and the cartilage. Do not implant near the head or the tip of the ear. Load the implant gun with the correct number of pellets. For example, Revalor-S has 10 pellets per dose. Push the needle through the skin at a shallow angle, then pull back slightly to create a pocket. Deposit the pellets in a straight line under the skin. Do not crush or break the pellets. Withdraw the needle and feel the pellets with your fingers to make sure they are in place. If you feel them under the skin, they are correct. If you cannot feel them, you may have injected too deep or missed. In that case, do not re-implant in the same ear. Use the other ear. Timing is critical. Implants are most effective when given to growing cattle. For steer fattening, implant at the start of the fattening period, usually when the steer weighs 250 to 300 kg. A second implant can be given 70 to 100 days later if the fattening period is longer than 120 days. Do not implant within 30 days of slaughter, because the hormones need time to work and to clear. Also, do not implant sick cattle or cattle with ear infections. Wait until they are healthy. Use a new needle for each animal or disinfect between animals to prevent spreading disease. After implanting, record the date, product, and ear used. Check the ear after a week for swelling or infection. If you see pus or swelling, consult a veterinarian. Proper technique ensures maximum growth response and avoids residue problems.

lessons.title: Effects on Growth Rate and Feed Efficiency
lessons.body: Growth promotants can significantly improve growth rate and feed efficiency, but the effects vary. Hormonal implants typically increase average daily gain (ADG) by 0.1 to 0.3 kg per day. For example, a steer gaining 1.0 kg per day without an implant might gain 1.2 to 1.3 kg per day with a good implant. Over a 120-day fattening period, that is an extra 24 to 36 kg of live weight. Feed efficiency also improves. Implants can reduce the feed required per kg of gain by 5 to 15%. If a steer needs 7 kg of feed per kg of gain without an implant, it might need 6 to 6.5 kg with an implant. That saves money on feed. Beta-agonists like zilpaterol have different effects. They are fed only in the last 20 to 40 days. They increase carcass weight by 5 to 15 kg and improve feed efficiency by 10 to 20% during that short period. They also increase muscle yield and reduce fat. However, beta-agonists can cause side effects like increased heart rate, tremors, and difficulty breathing. In some cases, they can cause lameness. These effects are more common in hot climates, so provide shade and plenty of water. The response to implants depends on the steer's genetics, nutrition, and health. Steers with high growth potential respond better. If feed is poor or cattle are sick, implants will not help much. Also, implants work best when cattle are on a high-energy diet, such as a feedlot ration with 70-80% grain. In Africa, many small-scale farmers use implants on pasture. The response is lower because pasture is lower in energy. For example, on good pasture, an implant might increase ADG by only 0.1 kg per day. On a feedlot ration, it could be 0.3 kg per day. To get the most from implants, combine them with good nutrition, clean water, and parasite control. Weigh your cattle regularly to track growth. If you see no improvement after 30 days, check your implant technique or feed quality. Remember, growth promotants are not magic. They are tools that work best with good management.

lessons.title: Consumer Perceptions and Market Acceptance
lessons.body: Consumer perceptions of growth promotants vary widely across Africa and the world. In many African countries, consumers are not aware of growth promotants. They buy meat based on price, appearance, and availability. However, in urban areas and for export markets, perceptions matter more. In South Africa, some consumers and retailers prefer meat from cattle raised without implants or beta-agonists. They may pay a premium for 'natural' or 'hormone-free' beef. In Europe, consumer opposition to hormonal implants and beta-agonists is very strong. The EU has banned these products since 1989. If you want to export to Europe, you cannot use them. Some African countries, like Namibia and Botswana, export beef to the EU. They have strict rules: no implants, no beta-agonists. Farmers must sign declarations and allow inspections. In contrast, markets in South Africa, Egypt, and some other countries accept meat from implanted cattle. But even there, some butcheries and supermarkets advertise 'no added hormones' to attract customers. Beta-agonists are more controversial than implants. Ractopamine is banned in many countries, including the EU, China, and Russia. Zilpaterol is allowed in South Africa but banned in the EU. If you use beta-agonists, you may lose access to certain markets. Consumer perception also affects local sales. In some communities, people believe that hormones in meat cause early puberty in children or other health problems. These beliefs may not be scientifically proven, but they influence buying decisions. As a farmer, you must know your market. If you sell directly to consumers at a local market, ask them what they prefer. If you sell to a feedlot or abattoir, ask about their requirements. Some buyers will test for residues. If you use growth promotants, be transparent. Label your meat if required. If you sell to a niche market, consider raising cattle without growth promotants. You can charge more for 'natural' beef. But your costs will be higher because growth is slower. Weigh the pros and cons. The key is to match your production method to your market's demands.

lessons.title: Alternatives to Hormonal Growth Promotants
lessons.body: If you cannot or do not want to use hormonal growth promotants, there are many alternatives to improve steer growth and feed efficiency. The most important is good nutrition. A well-balanced diet with enough energy, protein, minerals, and vitamins will maximize growth. For fattening steers, a ration with 70-80% grain (maize, sorghum, or barley) and 20-30% roughage (hay, silage) works well. Add a protein supplement like cottonseed cake or soybean meal. Provide a mineral lick with calcium, phosphorus, and trace minerals. Clean water is essential. A steer can drink 30-50 liters per day in hot weather. Without enough water, feed intake and growth drop. Another alternative is ionophores. These are feed additives like monensin (Rumensin) and lasalocid (Bovatec). They are not hormones. They improve feed efficiency by 5-10% and reduce bloat and coccidiosis. They are allowed in many African countries and are safe for consumers. Another option is probiotics and yeast cultures. These improve rumen health and digestion. They can increase feed efficiency by 2-5%. Also, consider genetic selection. Choose bulls with high growth rates and good feed efficiency. Use artificial insemination or buy bulls from reputable breeders. Crossbreeding with fast-growing breeds like Boran, Charolais, or Simmental can boost growth. Parasite control is critical. Internal parasites (worms) and external parasites (ticks) reduce growth. Deworm regularly and dip or spray for ticks. Vaccinate against common diseases like foot-and-mouth and lumpy skin disease. Good animal husbandry also helps. Reduce stress by handling cattle calmly. Provide shade and ventilation. Avoid overcrowding. Weigh cattle monthly to monitor growth. If growth is poor, check feed quality, health, and water. Finally, consider a longer fattening period. Without implants, steers may need 150-180 days to reach market weight instead of 120 days. But you save on the cost of implants and avoid market restrictions. Some farmers use a combination of these alternatives. For example, a feedlot in Kenya might use ionophores, good nutrition, and parasite control to achieve 1.0 kg per day without any hormones. That is profitable and meets market demands. Remember, the best alternative is always good management.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between hormonal implants and beta-agonists?
options: A) Implants are fed, beta-agonists are injected
B) Implants are placed under the skin of the ear, beta-agonists are fed
C) Implants are legal in the EU, beta-agonists are not
D) Implants are only for dairy cows, beta-agonists are for steers
quiz.explanation: Implants are placed under the skin of the ear, while beta-agonists are feed additives.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common hormonal implant brand used in steer fattening?
quiz.explanation: Revalor is a well-known hormonal implant brand; Zilmax and Paylean are beta-agonists, and Rumensin is an ionophore.

quiz.q: How much can a single Revalor-S implant increase daily weight gain?
quiz.explanation: A Revalor-S implant can increase daily gain by 0.2 to 0.3 kg over 90 to 120 days.

quiz.q: Which country in Africa has approved zilpaterol for use under strict withdrawal periods?
quiz.explanation: South Africa is the only African country that has approved zilpaterol for use with strict withdrawal periods.

quiz.q: Why are hormonal implants banned in the European Union?
options: A) They cause cancer in cattle
C) Consumer opposition and safety concerns
quiz.explanation: The EU banned hormonal implants due to consumer opposition and concerns about hormone residues.

quiz.q: What is a withdrawal period?
options: A) The time between implanting and slaughter
B) The time a drug must be stopped before slaughter to avoid residues
C) The time it takes for an implant to dissolve
D) The time cattle are kept off feed before slaughter
quiz.explanation: The withdrawal period is the time between the last administration of a drug and slaughter to ensure no residues remain.

quiz.q: For zilpaterol, what is the typical withdrawal period before slaughter?
quiz.explanation: Zilpaterol typically requires a withdrawal period of 3 to 7 days.

quiz.q: Where should implants be placed in a steer?
options: B) Under the skin of the ear
quiz.explanation: Implants must be placed under the skin of the ear, which is discarded at slaughter.

quiz.q: What tool is needed to implant cattle?
quiz.explanation: An implant gun is used to place pellets under the skin of the ear.

quiz.q: When is the best time to implant a steer for fattening?
quiz.explanation: Implants are most effective when given at the start of the fattening period, around 250-300 kg.

quiz.q: How many days before slaughter should you stop implanting?
quiz.explanation: Implants should not be given within 30 days of slaughter to allow hormones to clear.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot feel the implant pellets under the skin after implanting?
options: A) Re-implant in the same ear
quiz.explanation: If pellets are not felt, use the other ear to avoid over-dosing or improper placement.

quiz.q: How much can implants improve feed efficiency?
quiz.explanation: Implants can improve feed efficiency by 5 to 15%, reducing feed required per kg of gain.

quiz.q: What is a common side effect of beta-agonists like zilpaterol?
options: B) Increased heart rate and tremors
quiz.explanation: Beta-agonists can cause increased heart rate, tremors, and difficulty breathing, especially in hot climates.

quiz.q: Why do implants work better on a feedlot ration than on pasture?
options: A) Feedlot ration has more energy
quiz.explanation: Implants respond better when cattle are on a high-energy diet, such as a feedlot ration with 70-80% grain.

quiz.q: Which market is most likely to reject meat from cattle treated with beta-agonists?
options: A) Local butcher in South Africa
quiz.explanation: The European Union bans beta-agonists and will reject meat containing residues.

quiz.q: What is a major reason some African consumers prefer 'hormone-free' beef?
options: B) Beliefs about health risks, such as early puberty
quiz.explanation: Some consumers believe hormones in meat cause health problems like early puberty, influencing their buying decisions.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an alternative to hormonal growth promotants?
quiz.explanation: Ionophores like monensin are feed additives that improve feed efficiency without hormones.

quiz.q: What is the recommended grain percentage in a fattening ration for steers?
quiz.explanation: A fattening ration typically contains 70-80% grain and 20-30% roughage.

quiz.q: How much water can a steer drink per day in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: A steer can drink 30-50 liters of water per day in hot weather, which is essential for growth.

quiz.q: Which parasite control measure is important for steer growth?
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming controls internal parasites that reduce growth.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using ionophores in cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Ionophores improve feed efficiency by 5-10% and reduce bloat and coccidiosis.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record implant dates and withdrawal periods?
options: B) To avoid residue violations and meet market requirements
quiz.explanation: Keeping records helps ensure withdrawal periods are met and avoids residue problems that can lead to fines or rejected carcasses.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a beta-agonist?
quiz.explanation: Zilpaterol is a beta-agonist; Revalor and Synovex are implants, and monensin is an ionophore.

quiz.q: What is the main effect of beta-agonists on carcass composition?
options: B) Increase muscle yield and reduce fat
quiz.explanation: Beta-agonists redirect nutrients to muscle growth, increasing muscle yield and reducing fat.

quiz.q: How long is a typical fattening period for steers without implants?
quiz.explanation: Without implants, steers may need 150-180 days to reach market weight, compared to 120 days with implants.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a good practice when implanting cattle?
options: A) Clean the ear with iodine
B) Implant near the tip of the ear
C) Use a new needle for each animal
D) Feel for pellets after implanting
quiz.explanation: Implants should be placed in the middle third of the ear, not near the tip or head.

quiz.q: What is a potential consequence of using growth promotants without following regulations?
options: B) Fines or bans from selling
quiz.explanation: Non-compliance can lead to fines, rejected carcasses, or bans from selling to certain markets.

quiz.q: Which African country exports beef to the EU and therefore bans implants and beta-agonists?
quiz.explanation: Namibia exports beef to the EU and must follow EU rules, which ban implants and beta-agonists.

quiz.q: What is a practical alternative to implants for improving growth in steers?
options: B) Genetic selection for fast growth
quiz.explanation: Genetic selection for fast growth and feed efficiency is a viable alternative to hormonal implants.
